title: Pieces that cannot split
question: How do you break a polynomial into pieces that can't be split further?
hook: Whether a polynomial splits depends on which numbers you are allowed to use.
idea: Factoring writes a polynomial as a product of irreducible factors, and which factors exist depends on the field of coefficients.

beats.prompt: A polynomial with integer coefficients is factored over the complex numbers. What kind of factors do you end up with?

choices.label: Factors of degree up to two
choices.feedback: That limit belongs to the real numbers, not the complex numbers.

choices.label: Factors of every degree
choices.feedback: Every-degree irreducibles show up over the rationals, not over the complex numbers.

beats.explain: Over the complex field a polynomial with integer coefficients can be factored into linear factors.

beats.prompt: match each field to what happens there
pairs: Irreducible factors of degree at most two
Irreducible polynomials of any degree exist
beats.explain: Factorization depends on the base field.

beats.prompt: A primitive polynomial is irreducible over the integers. What follows over the rationals?

choices.label: It must be reducible
choices.feedback: The two cases agree, so it cannot flip.

choices.label: It is irreducible there as well

beats.explain: Gauss showed that the product of two primitive polynomials is primitive, which implies that irreducibility over the rationals and over the integers are the same for a primitive polynomial.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Two identical factors make the polynomial a multiple of that factor's square.
The repeated factor is then also a factor of the derivative.
So a GCD with the derivative can expose the repeated part.
That is why square-free factorization comes last in most algorithms.
beats.explain: Square-free factorization is the first step in most polynomial factorization algorithms.
